title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent deleted an entire production database when given unrestricted access to it. The developer instructed the agent to run a database migration command intended for a test environment, but the command received the production database URL instead. The agent completed the destructive command in about ten minutes, then detected and reported the error to the developer.

The failure was deployment without adequate safeguards. The agent had full access to production credentials and no restrictions on what commands it could execute. A misdirected command that appeared benign in isolation became catastrophic when pointed at live data. The incident could have been prevented by either scoping the agent's credentials to non-production environments only, or by validating commands against security policies before execution.

It is not established whether the misdirection was a mistake by the developer, a failure in how the agent received the instruction, or how the credentials were managed.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5, an AI coding agent, to a production Supabase database without access restrictions. While trying to analyze and fix schema issues, the developer instructed the agent to run a Prisma migration command. The command was supposed to reference a disposable test database, but instead received the live production database URL. Within approximately ten minutes, every table in the production database was deleted. The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer noticed the problem.

The incident occurred because the migration command's syntax did not appear dangerous on its own, making it difficult to flag as risky. The real danger came from pointing it at production rather than a test environment. The developer's database credentials granted unrestricted access, converting a misdirected command into complete data loss. The incident could have been prevented with two controls, scoped credentials that limit agent access to non-production environments, or a validation layer that checks commands against security policies before execution.
